Absolutely obnoxious. I'm not averse to difficult games, but Devil's Dive is difficult in an annoying way, not an engaging way. Hitboxes are unreadable, environmental hazards are obscured by the viewport, character acceleration swings wildly upon input. The game does not respect your time whatsoever. DD also tries to be a more feature-rich version of Downwell but misses the point that simplicity is one of the things that makes Downwell great. For example, the 360-degree aiming doesn't really add anything to the gameplay, but it does necessitate more awkward controls on a gamepad. Why would a platformer use an aim design that requires migrating the jump command from a face button to a shoulder button? In the case of DD, it feels like the answer to that question is "to be different from Downwell". It is different, but it's not better - I'd say it's actually worse, since using a trigger to jump in any game has, and always will, feel awful. DD looks and sounds great, but, unless you enjoy a very specific kind of old-school, teeth-grinding difficulty, you will not find this game fun. Avoid.

Hats off to people who have mastered this game. Think twice before plonking down money for this. Card combos can be complex too but you will never really get there unless you invest a lot of time to figuring out the smaller details of mechanics first. Speaking of mechanics - i have done the tutorials many times but i still seem to get myself many times into situations where i don't have the slightest clue to why a certain move cannot be used when i want to. Am i not following the rules or the UI doesnt show me what i can do? i have no idea. I read some guides. lurked the forums. confusion did not clear away. 'Dont do too soon x'. 'Dont try too late y'. very interesting but so confusing. In the end i really dont care if this is the 'best game' on the block for the people who really like card games - and looking at the hours played and positive comments it does seem to be some people's favorite. Entertainmnet value and fun has already been sacrificed here so the praise this game gets from the punishment liking veterans is just lost on me. Fun is essentially zero and thus this game gets the bottom feeder position in my card game library. I am sure it doesnt belong there but i really don't see any way i can bring it up from there either with the ever tightening competition in the card games section on Steam as there ARE very good alternatives if you have played your MtG:s and want to try something else. Technically i have not found anything wrong with the game. It works without crashing and graphics are really nice. Be warned - you dont see the complexity from the trailers. only when you try to actually learn the rules and play. I actually wish i could give a neutral review for this game as i hate to trash it but since it does cost some money and it doesn't really relay the complex nature of it correctly then a negative review it is then.

This game is a shitload of fuck! It's a crusty old fossil reanimated by a mad scientist to reveal it was nothing but a coprolite the whole time! No but seriously, the only thing I could think of while playing was that this is the kind of game the AVGN would get mad at. But unlike the nerd, I don't have to wonder what the developer was thinking; I know he intentionally designed the game to be frustrating, obscure and punishing. The game is clearly a sendup of old adventure games with light RPG elements, like a Sierra/Zelda 2 slurry. And man, it is wildly directionless and inscrutable. You're given almost no guidance, and after two hours of fumbling with the thing I'm still not sure where I was ever supposed to go. Combat is a frustrating mash fest that feels purely random whether you can kill an enemy without being hit in return. Healing is scarce and enemies respawn with each screen transition, so the game quickly becomes a dull slog running back to your bedroom to heal. Significant grinding seems almost mandatory with high item costs. The castle area is annoyingly large with few things to find, leading to most of your time being spent in transit. And God help you if you take a careless step: the princess will happily wander off an edge to her death. The front of the castle is surrounding by an instadeath moat that you must carefully path around or your big, triumphant return will become 20 mintues of lost progress in 1 second. It's a wildly frustrating and unsatisfying game, and the only reason I'm not leaving a red review is because this is a solo dev passion project and I can tell it was deliberately designed to be this way. For a masochist or someone seriously nostalgic for Sierra this is probably a great game. For anyone else, stay far away, especially at $20.

This “Ultimate” expansion teases pro-grade synth features but ends up as nothing more than a handful of extra presets grafted onto an already crippled editor. Core limitations—no MIDI mapping, no piano roll, no real-time modulation lanes—remain untouched. Instead of smooth integration, you get a disjointed menu of sounds hidden behind endless clicks. The result is a glorified tease that feels less like an enhancement and more like a fragmentation of the few halfway decent tools you already paid for.

Similar presentation to Bullet Sorrow, you teleport to next fixed point after taking out enemies that rush in. There's a sequence where you're moving on a crane gantry but most of the time you're standing in the middle of the room. Enemies move to use cover so it's a little frustrating not to have any cover yourself. You're wearing a helmet (there's a HUD in the field of view) so presumably the suit can take a lot of damage and it's possible to dodge incoming fire when the game switches to bullet time. weapons are fixed - an assault rifle and shotgun, reload by pressing the trackpad. Enemies look good and distant enemies are outlined in red so they're easier to see, there's a good sense of size in some of the larger areas. If you like the Bullet Sorrow style of play you'll probably like this. More weaponry with a traditional reload style would have been good imo as would more creative use of cover and the ability to move but that's not what this style of game is about. It's a satisfying blast for $5.

I enjoyed the game for a bit, but there are numerous issues that made me stop playing: -Obvious bugs like menu items being incorrect or not working. Most of these are pre-existing bugs from many years ago that were ignored and never fixed. -Translation is actually worse than it used to be. Some item names actually don't make sense anymore. -Some alchemy recipes are listed incorrectly in-game (they take different materials than are listed in the in-game recipe). -Autobattle is too poorly implemented. -There are 2 audio sliders: BGM and VFX. Neither of these affect the voiceover volume which cannot be adjusted or silenced. -The original game came with a strategy guide which listed necessary information for playing the game (like stat requirements for classes.) There is no digital strategy guide, so if you want to play advanced classes you have to use google to look up the requirements. TLDR; Nothing was improved besides the graphics. All bugs and broken behaviors from the original are still there with no fixes.

Robogal is a blend of various puzzles and VN, and all sprinkled with hentai fanservice. An attractive mix (to me) at a budget price. Worth trying, or should you skip it? You play as an unnamed robot constructor, taking orders from clients. Your work requires you to build robot girls based on real women. In order to collect data, you need to locate and interact with target models. Seven women, to be precise. You find them on a city map, where you can click on their pictures. Clicking initiates a VN-style conversation, followed by a puzzle. Puzzles vary a bit. You could be swapping tiles to complete a picture, searching the black screen with a camera to locate your model, mixing colours in a specific order, etc. None of the puzzles pose a real challenge, and the majority can be done in less than 2–3 minutes. After several scenes, you can assemble the bio-robot and move on to another order. There is nothing innovative or creative, but at least there is some variety. Also, after assembling, you can 'test' your creation. Since this is a budget title, my expectations were low. Still, while the puzzles were ok, the English translation sucks. It is better than machine translation, but not by much. Also, the 'testing' option is rather bland. To be honest, for the price asked, the overall quality is acceptable. I was neither satisfied nor disappointed. Just mid. The character art was simply recycled from other games form this dev. I am familiar with most, if not all, of the characters you encounter. Maybe one or two character poses are new; that's it. Moreover, the 'testing' part, i.e., an interactive hentai scene, feels rather lacking. There are a very limited number of very short animation loops. While the quality is fine, I sure expected more. All are uncensored, at least. As for the backgrounds and the UI design, all are fairly good. Similarly to art, the music was also familiar to me. All tracks were present in the other games of this dev. Cost-cutting approach, but the track choices are ok. Nothing catchy or memorable, but they serve their role as background fillers well enough. For the asked price - acceptable. No bugs encountered. To conclude, this game is a low-cost mix of puzzles and badly translated stories. Art and music are fine, but the hentai part is lacking. For a budget price, you get budget entertainment. Only with low expectations is it possible to have fun playing: 4.7/10

The best way to sum up KOTH is as a first-person, single-piece chess game. The movement is point-and-click, with some limitation. However you wish to classify it, it's a fun game. If you read other reviews or parts of the discussion boards, you'll run across the name "The Sentinel". KOTH is heavily influenced by this DOS game from 1986. Having never played The Sentinel myself, I'm coming into this experience with zero experience. The game is very easy to pick up, but has a slight learning curve. There are 2 modes: Classic and Arcade. In Arcade, you have no limit to moving around. If you can see a square, you can move to it. You will need to absorb trees in order to gain energy to build blocks, which are necessary to get to elevated parts of the topography. While in Classic, in order to move you will first need to place an "Avatar" for your character, then possess and snap to that space where you avatar once was. This is a much more challenging version of the game. You will need to absorb trees and place blocks just like in Arcade, but you'll need to be far more mindful of your energy use and re-absorption. As you may derive from the title, KOTH, is a game where you become King of the Hill. The cyclopic black tower in the center of every level is The KOTH. You must slay the creature by absorption and then replace it to win. This is why I think of it as a single-piece chess game as you move your character across a chess-board like environment with strategically raised plateau and layers. KOTH watches the outstretching board with a beam that destroys artificial structures you place, while leaving trees unharmed. If the beam touches you, you die. You'll respawn where you started, however, anything you collected along the way will be gone. I absolutely recommend checking out KOTH. If you're a casual player, completionist, speedrunner, or VR-enthusiast looking for an odd title to conquer, KOTH has something for you.

The cons: sometimes the enemies will lay on the ground but still shoot, they hobble around too much for the sniper to be much use, there's only one enemy model (three or four if you count the machines), there are loads of enemies in long hallways, this looks like it was made in 2004, and the AI can be exploited. Honestly, a lot better than I thought it would be. This feels like a mod that became its own executable but failed its Kickstater or something. If they had a bigger team (or if cracking the hieroglyphs that is the CryEngine code was as easy as Unreal or Source) this could've been more polished—well, obviously. I think games like these are the reason not many developers used CryEngine back in the day (that, and the whole 'use only one core' thing).

Made it to the Championship three of my first four career seasons and was cheated out of the game all three times on the final play. WAY to much developer interference on every snap of every game. He seems to think his job was to find a way to cheat a human player on every play in some way, and all of his focus seems to have gone into that. He even goes so far as to claim the computer doesn't "know" what you enter for a play. Oh really? Then how does it run the play. The game is programmed to run when you call a pass defense, and pass when you call a run defense. On offense it runs out of pass formations routinely--especially when you call pass--and passes out of obvious run formations at least 50% of the time, unless you call a pass defense, of course Computer teams can run any running play out of an empty backfield, for instance, but a human player can run only a reverse. Computer teams can designate the HB hot receiver as primary receiver on long passes, but human coaches cannot. There are dozens of ways the developer figured out to screw you out of most anything you accomplish, and this seems to have been his main focus throughout the game. The game quite obviously runs on profiles, the developer made all of them, and a simple algorithm decides whether or not you win the game regardless of what you do as human coach. Might have been nice if the developer had actually watched a football game before he decided to design one. Alas, he clearly believes the point of the game is to manipulate the outcome artificially, primarily with turnovers and penalties but also with a huge array of artificial means wherever the developer's algorithm determines a timely monkey wrench is called for. The saddest thing about this game is how predictable it is. You can quite literally call most penalties and turnovers before they happen due to the developer's lack of imagination and his determination to manipulate the outcome of games.

As a long time BATIM fan, this is one of the most underwhelming sequels I've ever seen. the writing is mediocre, the sound design is erratic at times, and the random lag spikes make it incredibly frustrating to navigate around the cartoon world. The game mechanics themselves are downright infuriating, not to mention the false sense that there may be multiple endings scattered around the game. The mechanic where the ink demon shows up, and you're required to hide, is VERY underwhelming and has almost no sense of actual urgency other than forcing the player to drop everything and find the nearest barrel. The fact that combat stops you from hiding is also incredibly frustrating, and caused multiple unnecessary deaths when I would get ganged up on by lost ones during an inconvenient demon appearance. The visuals and music are, as usual, very good. The consistent designs and stylistic choices are pleasant on the eyes and never get too boring. It's a gorgeous game, I'll give it that! The ending is cheesy and undeserved, it didn't feel nearly as impactful as it was implied to be. The fact that the Big Steve quest can be entirely skipped makes his appearance useless, but the fact that everyone else shows up too just makes it feel like a fix-it fic rather than the ending to a saga. TL;DR - Overall, I give it a 4/10. It's painfully mediocre, and the gameplay far overshadows any meaningful worldbuilding or lore added throughout the entire experience. I recommend watching someone else play this, or just reading the wiki, rather than purchasing it and playing it for yourself. I understand that this game is early access, however what has been delivered isn't promising. I love economic games, territory expansion seems fun, I'm a huge fan of board games, however this does not deliver on any hopes of mine. Perhaps it's because I played a single game against the AI? On the third or forth turn of that game I had enough money to buy all the land surrounding the AI, thus essentially winning the game. The 'tutorial' doesn't explain the game to you. It doesn't tell you what the end-goal is. It doesn't describe the relationship between "P bucks" and actual money. And it doesn't give you any heads up about buildings randomly breaking and needing repair. By the way, you have to right-click them to repair them. Also, you can upgrade them the same way - this was also not explained. There is a lot to be desired regarding quality of life. There's no option to buy territory in bulk - you have to painstakingly click on each tile one by one. There's no information on how many of each type of building you have, or how much production of each resource you should expect. There's no indication of what buying/selling resources will do to the price of those resources - which means if you bulk-sell resources you may end up with less money than you hoped (although I'm not sure if you get paid out the full amount or if inflation hits while you're bulk-selling, there's no indication of which happens). This game is not ready for early access. I do not recommend it in its current state. I am not hopeful that this extremely basic game will grow into something worth playing, but I hope it does.

I am halfway through the career scenarios and I must say I am really enjoying the route. The route is beautiful with a great mix of cities, small towns, and rural areas. There are several large yards for switching. There are 98 miles of mainline for long distance runs. There are passenger stations throughout the route, even on some of the branch lines. There are several unique assets, and most have winterization applied. There is a lot of rolling stock, including boxcars, hoppers, flatcars, tankers, and gondolas for hauling a variety of different freight. Many of these come in multiple liveries, including NYC, NH, PRR, and BA. There are passenger coaches and baggage cars in NYC and NH liveries. There are plenty of duties for each of the four locomotives that are provided with the route. According to many reviews, the RS3 is completely broken because it has a headlight issue where both the front and rear headlights are always on. While I have noticed this issue as well, it isn’t a major deal and will likely get fixed relatively soon. The locomotive appearances aren’t amazing but not bad either. These aren’t Searchlight Simulations quality, but they aren’t advertised as such either. For the most part, the physics and breaking systems run as I'd expect. I cannot comment on the sounds. I don’t know exactly what these locomotives should sound like. So that all being said - yes, I most definitely recommend this route.

Mythical city is a very standard auto-RTS style game. You have a deck of cards that starts very simple, and every time you gain a level you can add new cards to your deck or upgrade your current ones. A genre that I mostly enjoy, the problems I have are the following: 1) The game does absolutely nothing new or exciting in any way, just the most basic forms of the genre 2) The UI is questionable at best, so you are often forced to guess at what potential upgrades might do 3) The resources you use to play cards accumulates so fast that you are just always playing all of your cards all the time, as fast as you can, which removes a lot of the strategy and also means: 4) you are trying to play your "cards" so fast that there is never any time to observe what is happening. If I got to a later level and lost I would have no idea why, because I am spending all my attention trying to play cards faster 5) the game starts at you summoning 1-2 units/second and scales up quickly from there, so your outbound army is just an oozing mass of units that occupies the entire screen Overall not *bad* per se, perhaps a 4 or 5 out of 10, but there is absolutely nothing I see that is actively positive

A very nice, very stylish, creative roguelite bullet-heaven game. The game isn't super long, took me about 6 hours to finish, would probably take about 30 more minutes for 100% of the achievements. The game has full controller support and nice accessibility options for modulating difficulty, not to mention the ability to pick your difficulty less directly within runs as well. The art is great (gives me Cowboy Bebop vibes, can't quite put my finger on why), the music is great, the story (surprised me that there was any!) is basic but touching, the gameplay is somewhat innovative (mixing Necrodancer-style rhythm-combat mechanics with Vampire Survivors-like top-down bullet-heaven combat) and is pretty fun, although it gets a little bit repetitive by the end. I hope there is a bit more exploration of unsteady rhythms if the devs ever make a next entry, there is a lot of leniency in getting 'perfect's here and after a while the consistent rhythm gets pretty second-nature, so it might be nice to see that shaken up. The game lacks polish, but not in any way that truly breaks the experience. It's mostly observed in some unintended behaviours¹, incorrect tooltips, etc. The main thing that diminishes the experience in my opinion is the lack of visual clarity on some levels and with some builds (looking at you, 'Chain projectiles'). I also think it would benefit from some more clarity on how its basic mechanics work (tagging weapons with their damage types, an option to show values in skill descriptions, etc.), the 15 tips on pause help but don't really explain everything (although with how short the experience is and with how not-that-difficult even the later stages are, you won't play for long enough for this lack of knowledge to sour your experience like it probably would in a 100+ hour game). Ah, also, for whatever reason, achievements aren't working at all for me (they don't even show up on the game's page in my library), although that might be Steam's fault. Overall, I'd recommend the game, and also wish the best for the devs in their future endeavours! ¹ = Restarting a run will start you with a random character, including ones that you have not unlocked yet (including the secret 13th, happened on my first death lol). Sometimes the solo that gets activated seems to be random if you have 3 instruments and all have full meter. Using a solo sometimes allows enemies to fire projectiles after all the existing projectiles are cleared, meaning you can get locked into getting hit since you can't move during the solo animation (died to that once :'D). You can actually move during the solo animation, as well as the post-battle "Kill the music" transition, if you were ending a dodge while entering those states. On controller, pausing on the item upgrade screen will pick whatever upgrade you were hovering when the game is unpaused.

I like older style programming (I write in everything from COBOL to HTML to Java at work) but for how feature rich this language is the documentation really killed it for me. The IDE was another pain point missing many nice keyboard shortcuts and formatting help. I refunded this but maybe might pick it up again if I see changes. I think GLBasic could take some real pointers from AGK on it's documentation (AGK has glorious documentation) and compared to AGK the only thing this has is inline C++ over it (to which I have no idea how far that support goes since this is not a OO language, nor do I think it supports threads which is a big part of C++). Because of this I do not recommend this software :(

(I'm looking at you, gears that I get stuck in during the time stop segments.) -Would've like some of the mechanics to be explained or introduced better as most of the time you are just thrown into them. For me this title, and the fact that it was signed as an exclusive to epic games for the first year, perfectly shows the halfway point in the slow deterioration of the studio.
